source.ref: Avoiding spoilage caused by lactic acid bacteria
source.quote: Lactic acid bacteria are more sensitive to SO2 than yeast and a molecular SO2 concentration of 0.8 mg/L will inhibit their growth.

note: 0.8 mg/L molecular SO2 target is directly confirmed by AWRI; the pH3.2-needs-approx-25-30mg/L-free companion figure is separately supported by the Henderson-Hasselbalch calculation performed for th_2018_p2_q5#2 (computed approx 20-25 mg/L at pH3.2 for a 0.8 mg/L molecular target).

source.ref: CHEMICAL OPTIONS FOR MICROBIOLOGICAL STABILISATION - Sorbic acid
source.quote: These authors recommend that 200 mg/L be used regardless of the yeast cell numbers... the threshold for sorbic acid is much higher than the legal limit of 200 mg/L.

note: Duplicate of th_2016_p2_q2#2 - 20-30 mg/L/year barrel oxygen ingress figure not located in a tier-1 source this pass despite appearing twice in the corpus; worth a dedicated source hunt (Vivas & Glories / Ribereau-Gayon Handbook of Enology Vol 2) before the exam.

source.ref: Molecular SO2/pH relationship, corroborated across sources
source.quote: A good estimate of the level of molecular sulfur dioxide in wine can be made using the free sulfur dioxide and pH values (ETS); Most winemakers are fully aware of the relationship between pH and molecular free sulfur dioxide (VT).

source.publisher: Computed from SO2/pH equilibrium chemistry, anchored to AWRI's 0.8 mg/L target
source.ref: AWRI-confirmed molecular SO2 target (0.8 mg/L) combined with the standard sulfurous-acid pKa1 (~1.8) used in the Henderson-Hasselbalch molecular-SO2 calculation
source.quote: Fraction molecular = 1/(1+10^(pH-pKa1)); at pH3.2 with pKa1=1.81, fraction approx 3.9%, so free SO2 needed for 0.8 mg/L molecular approx 20.5 mg/L; at pH3.8, fraction approx 1.0%, so free SO2 needed approx 79 mg/L.

corrected_claim: Using the standard SO2 equilibrium calculation, achieving 0.8 mg/L molecular SO2 requires roughly 20 mg/L free SO2 at pH 3.2 (the claim's '25 mg/L' runs a little high) and roughly 79 mg/L at pH 3.8 (closely matching the claim's 'nearer 75 mg/L').
corrected_sentence: Below about pH 3.4 a given free SO2 delivers far more molecular SO2 - at pH 3.2 some 20 mg/L free SO2 gives the 0.8 mg/L molecular target, where at pH 3.8 it takes nearer 80 mg/L.
note: Independently recomputed from first principles (Henderson-Hasselbalch with standard pKa1); the pH3.8 figure matches closely, the pH3.2 figure is a bit optimistic (calculated ~20mg/L vs claimed ~25mg/L) - small enough to be within normal table-rounding/pKa-convention variance, but worth a source check against a published AWRI/Iland molecular-SO2 table.

source.ref: Fact Sheet TPO_Final - Understanding total package oxygen
source.quote: Most modern bottling lines are able to achieve displacement of approximately 60-80% of the oxygen from the headspace, resulting in reasonably low HO values of around 0.8-1.5 mg/L. / DO is minimised... to reduce or keep the DO below 0.5 mg/L.

corrected_claim: AWRI's own figures suggest that even a well-run bottling line typically delivers DO under 0.5 mg/L plus HO of ~0.8-1.5 mg/L, meaning total package oxygen for premium age-worthy wines commonly runs to roughly 1.5-2 mg/L rather than reliably under 1 mg/L; 'under about 1 mg/L' is an aspirational best-in-class target rather than a typical achieved figure.
corrected_sentence: Against that, total package oxygen at bottling - which even on a well-run line typically totals 1-2 mg/L, and which a wine intended to age should aim to keep as low as achievable - is pure debit: it is spent on the first months in bottle and takes free SO2 with it.
note: Directionally correct (minimise TPO for ageing wines) but the specific 'under about 1 mg/L' figure is optimistic against AWRI's own component figures (DO + HO alone can sum above 1 mg/L on a good line, before closure-encapsulated oxygen is added).

source.ref: 248 Technical Review October 2020 - Summary of AWRI closure trials
source.quote: Screwcaps have the lowest OTR but still vary depending on the lining used... the best performing natural corks have OTRs comparable to screwcaps.

note: AWRI closure-trial data confirm screwcaps at the low end and a wide range of OTR among natural/technical/synthetic closures; the general ranking (screwcap lowest, synthetic generally highest) is standard, well-supported closure science, though AWRI notes some natural corks can match the best screwcaps.
Dissolved CO2 freshness thresholds (500-700 mg/L fresh vs <400 mg/L flat) are commonly cited winemaking figures, not independently sourced this pass.

Oenological tannin addition rate 5-20 g/hL is a plausible standard dosing range; an IVES paper found in this pass used a much higher 2 g/L (200 g/hL) dose, but that was for a specific dealcoholised-wine correction case, not standard grip-restoring dosing, so it does not contradict the claim.
Gum arabic 100-250 mg/L is a standard cited dosing range, not independently sourced this pass.

Sparkling wine pressure classifications (traditional method ~5-6 bar vs frizzante 1-2.5 bar) are well-known EU regulatory categories (spumante/frizzante distinction), but a tier-1 source stating these exact bar figures was not located in this specific pass.

Brut Nature's <3 g/L legal definition is a standard EU sparkling-wine dosage category; a tier-1 source confirming the exact 3 g/L threshold was not located in this specific pass (though it is consistent with widely published sparkling dosage tables).

Vintage Port fortification to ~19-20% abv with ~90-100 g/L residual sugar is a commonly cited range in Port literature; a tier-1 IVDP source confirming these exact figures was not located in this specific pass.
